bai.moTa: The 1919 eclipse, the Shapiro delay, gravitational lensing, the photon sphere
bai.yChinh: Light has no mass, yet it still follows the geodesics of curved spacetime, the kind of path with $\dd s^2 = 0$. Passing a mass, a light ray is bent toward it, by **twice** the angle Newton’s theory gives, because both time and space are curved. It also arrives later (the Shapiro delay), produces Einstein rings, and close to a black hole it can circle at 1.5 rs.
bai.giaiThich:
- Light follows null geodesics: $\dd s^2 = 0$ at every point along the path.
    - Deflection angle in weak gravity: $\alpha = 4GM/(c^2b) = 2r_s/b$. Grazing the Sun’s edge: 1.75″; Newton gives only 0.88″. Half comes from curved time, half from curved space.
    - The 1919 eclipse expeditions organized by Dyson and Eddington measured 1.98″ (Sobral) and 1.61″ (Príncipe).
    - Radar signals passing close to the Sun arrive about 250 microseconds late (the Shapiro delay); in 2002 the Cassini spacecraft checked this to 2 parts in a hundred thousand.
    - Gravitational lensing: when everything lines up, the image becomes an Einstein ring of radius $\theta_E = \sqrt{4GM D_{LS}/(c^2 D_L D_S)}$.
    - The photon sphere lies at 1.5 rs; rays with an impact parameter below $(3\sqrt3/2)\,r_s \approx 2{,}6\,r_s$ are swallowed.
bai.conSo.1: **1.75″**: the deflection of a ray grazing the Sun’s edge, about 1/2000 of a degree. Newton: 0.88″.
bai.conSo.2: **29 May 1919**: the eclipse seen from Sobral and Príncipe; the measurements were 1.98″ ± 0.12″ and 1.61″ ± 0.30″.
bai.conSo.3: **About 250 microseconds**: how late a radar signal to Mars arrives when it passes close to the Sun (there and back).
bai.conSo.4: **2.6 rs** (exactly $3\sqrt3/2$): the critical impact parameter. **1.5 rs**: the photon sphere.
bai.hieuDung: **Light does not “slow down” where it is.** Anyone who measures the speed of light right next to them gets exactly $c$, even close to a black hole. The Shapiro delay exists because clocks and rulers in strong gravity differ from those far away. And light is not bent because it “has weight”: it travels straight through curved spacetime.
bai.nguon: 1919 eclipse: Dyson, Eddington and Davidson 1920. Shapiro delay proposal: Shapiro 1964. Cassini measurement: Bertotti, Iess and Tortora 2003, Nature 425, 374. Constants: CODATA 2018, IAU 2012. The rays in the model are numerical solutions of the Schwarzschild null geodesic equation.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.1: Explain, using the idea of a “null geodesic”, why massless light is still bent.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.2: Calculate the deflection $2r_s/b$ at the Sun’s edge and explain why it is twice the Newtonian value.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.3: Describe the 1919 eclipse measurement and the Shapiro delay measurement, with their numbers.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.4: Use the Einstein-radius formula to estimate the size of an Einstein ring.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.5: Explain the photon sphere at 1.5 rs and the critical impact parameter of 2.6 rs.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
A beam of parallel light rays travels from left to right, past a black hole. Each golden strand is **a ray computed from the equations**, not a hand-drawn line. The closer a ray passes, the more it bends; rays that pass too close fall in (shown in red).

In Lesson 5, light had a world line tilted at exactly 45°: the spacetime interval along it is 0. In curved spacetime that is still true, but only **bit by bit**, at every point along the path:

$$ \dd s^2 = 0 $$

The path that satisfies this and is as “straight” as possible is a {{đường trắc địa kiểu ánh sáng|null geodesic}}. Light does not need mass to be bent: it simply goes straight through curved spacetime.

The equivalence principle (Lesson 7) already hinted at this: in an accelerating elevator, a light beam fired sideways seems to curve downward. In 1911 Einstein used exactly that idea to calculate the deflection. His number was only **half** the correct value; the next step explains why.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the blue dot on the selected ray up and down to change where it passes. Behind, the whole starry sky is bent by the same angles: the dense ring of stars around the black shadow is made of images of stars lying right behind the black hole. As you drag, a tone rises with the deflection (one octave for every 90°) and slides down when the ray is swallowed; the sound is only an illustration.
> [[Mass off|m0]] [[Medium mass|m1]] [[Large mass|m2]]

+++ Going deeper: how the model computes each ray
For light in the Schwarzschild geometry, set $u = 1/r$. The path satisfies

$$ \frac{\dd^2u}{\dd\varphi^2} + u = \frac32\,r_s\,u^2 $$

With no mass ($r_s = 0$) the solution is $u = \sin\varphi/b$: a straight line at distance $b$ from the center. The right-hand side is the part of the curvature that bends the ray.

This equation gives the same path shape as a “particle” moving through flat space with acceleration $\vec a = -\frac32 r_s h^2\,\vec x/r^5$, where $h$ is the impact parameter times the speed. The model solves that equation for each ray with the fourth-order Runge–Kutta method, a few hundred steps per ray.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
Now we look straight down onto the plane of the beam. The blue ray is the selected ray. The dashed gray line is the path Newton’s theory gives if light is treated as a bullet flying at speed $c$. The faint straight blue line is the path with no mass at all.

When a ray passes far from the mass (weak gravity), Einstein gives a deflection

$$ \alpha = \frac{4GM}{c^2b} = \frac{2r_s}{b} $$

$b$ is the {{khoảng ngắm|impact parameter}}: the distance from the center to the ray’s original line of flight. Newton gives only $r_s/b$, exactly half.

> [Ví dụ] For $b = 8\,r_s$: the formula gives 14.3°; the model’s exact calculation gives 17.8° (close to a black hole the approximate formula falls short); Newton gives only 7.2°. For $b = 14\,r_s$: formula 8.2°, exact 9.2°.

Why twice? Half of the deflection comes from **curved time** (Lesson 9), the part that both the equivalence principle and Newton “see”. The other half comes from **curved space** (Lesson 11): rulers stretch near the mass. A slow object hardly notices the second half, because it travels a little through space and a lot through time; light travels through space exactly as much as through time.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the blue dot at the start of the selected ray: farther out, the deflection shrinks roughly as $1/b$; closer in, the exact value pulls far ahead of the formula.
> [[Impact parameter 4 rs|b4]] [[8 rs|b8]] [[14 rs|b14]]

+++ Going deeper: the two halves of the deflection
In weak gravity the metric is approximately ($\Phi = -GM/r$ is the Newtonian potential)

$$ \dd s^2 = -\Big(1+\frac{2\Phi}{c^2}\Big)c^2\dd t^2 + \Big(1-\frac{2\Phi}{c^2}\Big)\dd\ell^2 $$

For light $\dd s = 0$, so the “apparent” coordinate speed is $\dd\ell/\dd t \approx c\,(1 + 2\Phi/c^2)$. It is like light passing through glass with refractive index $n \approx 1 - 2\Phi/c^2$: one part $-\Phi/c^2$ comes from the coefficient of $\dd t^2$, and an equal part from the coefficient of $\dd\ell^2$.

A ray bends toward higher refractive index; the deflection is the integral of the sideways gradient of the index along the path:

$$ \alpha = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{2GMb}{c^2(b^2+x^2)^{3/2}}\,\dd x = \frac{4GM}{c^2b} $$

Keeping only the coefficient of $\dd t^2$ (as Einstein did in 1911) gives half that: $2GM/(c^2b)$.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.thuThach.de: Drag the selected ray until its numerically computed deflection (data box, “Einstein” line) reaches **20°** (within 1°). What does the formula $2r_s/b$ give then, and what does Newton give?
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.thuThach.goiY: At $b = 8\,r_s$ the ray bends 17.8°; you need to come in a little closer, to about $b \approx 7{,}3\,r_s$. There the formula gives about 15.7°, and Newton only about 7.9°.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
Apply the formula to the Sun. The Sun’s radius is about **235,600 times** its Schwarzschild radius (2.95 km). Light from a star grazing the Sun’s edge is bent by

$$ \alpha = \frac{2r_s}{b} = \frac{2\times 2{,}95\ \text{km}}{695\,700\ \text{km}} $$

$$ \alpha = 8{,}5\times10^{-6}\ \text{rad} = 1{,}75″ $$

That is about one two-thousandth of a degree. Newton gives 0.88″.

Light is bent **toward** the Sun, so we see the star shifted **away from** the Sun compared with its usual position. To photograph stars right next to the Sun, you have to wait for a total solar eclipse.

> [Lịch sử] On 29 May 1919, two expeditions organized by Frank Dyson, one of them led by Arthur Eddington, photographed the stars around the Sun during the eclipse from Sobral (Brazil) and the island of Príncipe (off the coast of Africa). They compared these with photographs of the same patch of sky taken at night, when the Sun was elsewhere (a few months before or after the eclipse). The results, published in 1920: **1.98″ ± 0.12″** at Sobral and **1.61″ ± 0.30″** at Príncipe. Both matched Einstein, not Newton. The news made Einstein famous around the world.

> [Lưu ý] The 1919 uncertainties were still large, and one set of plates had to be discarded because of a technical fault. Later measurements with radio telescopes settled the result for good. In the model, the “mass” is far stronger than the Sun so that the deflection is large enough to see.

> [Thử ngay] [[Compare with Newton|nbat]] [[Off|ntat]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.ten: The Shapiro delay: light arrives late
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
The **bright dots** are flashes emitted all at once on the left, traveling along the rays. Joining the dots of the same flash gives a **wavefront**. Watch the wavefront as it passes the mass: the part that passes close **lags behind**. By the distant clock, light crossing a region of strong gravity takes longer.

In 1964 Irwin Shapiro proposed measuring this: bounce radar off a planet lying almost behind the Sun and time how long the echo takes to come back. The extra delay, there and back, is

$$ \Delta t \approx \frac{4GM}{c^3}\,\ln\frac{4r_1r_2}{b^2} $$

$r_1$ and $r_2$ are the distances from the Sun to Earth and to the planet, and $b$ is the signal’s closest distance to the center of the Sun.

> [Ví dụ] For the Sun, $4GM/c^3$ is 19.7 microseconds. For Mars ($r_2 = 1{,}52$ AU) and a signal grazing the Sun’s edge, the logarithm is about 12.5, so the signal arrives about **250 microseconds** late.

> [Lịch sử] In the late 1960s, Shapiro’s group measured the delay with radar echoes from Venus and Mercury. In 2002, radio signals from the Cassini spacecraft (on its way to Saturn) matched Einstein’s prediction to about **2 parts in a hundred thousand** (published in 2003).

> [Thử ngay] Listen to the imaginary “receiver” on the right: the high “tick” marks when a flash would have arrived without the mass, and the low note marks when the flash on the selected ray actually arrives. The low note always comes after the high one; the gap between them is that ray’s delay (including both the longer path and the Shapiro delay; the sound is only an illustration, and the flashes in the model are slowed down enormously).
> [[Slow flashes|cham]] [[Freeze the flashes|dung]] [[Normal speed|chay]]

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] “Light slows down near the Sun.” Anyone who measures the speed of light right next to them gets exactly $c$. The delay comes from clocks and rulers near the Sun differing from those far away.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.ten: Gravitational lensing and the Einstein ring
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
Seen from behind the mass, rays on every side are bent inward and brought together, as if by a lens. That is {{thấu kính hấp dẫn|gravitational lensing}}.

The small panel **“The sky the observer sees”** under Model controls shows the result: a distant galaxy (the small yellow dot is its true position) lying behind the mass appears as **two images**, one outside and one inside on the opposite side. When everything lines up, the two images smear into a single **{{vòng Einstein|Einstein ring}}** of radius

$$ \theta_E = \sqrt{\frac{4GM}{c^2}\,\frac{D_{LS}}{D_L\,D_S}} $$

$D_L$: distance to the lens, $D_S$: to the source, $D_{LS}$: from the lens to the source.

> [Ví dụ] A star as heavy as the Sun at 4 kpc, in front of a star at 8 kpc: $\theta_E \approx 1$ milliarcsecond, too small to see a ring; we only see the background star **brighten** for a few weeks. A galaxy of $10^{12}$ solar masses at 1 Gpc, with the source at 2 Gpc: $\theta_E \approx 2″$, large enough for the Hubble and James Webb telescopes to photograph the ring clearly.

> [Thử ngay] We are standing exactly where the small panel’s observer stands. Drag the yellow dot (the true position of the background galaxy, behind the black hole) to the middle: in the sky behind, the galaxy’s image bends into two arcs and then closes into a ring. A tone rises with the combined brightness of the two images; when they line up, a bell rings (the sound is only an illustration).
> [[Line up|thang]] [[Offset by 0.35 Einstein radii|lech]] [[Far off|xa]]

> [Lưu ý] The small panel uses the weak-field lens equation for a point mass, $\beta = \theta - \theta_E^2/\theta$, in units of $\theta_E$. With the source offset by 0.35 $\theta_E$, the two images are at 1.19 and −0.84 $\theta_E$.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.de: **Drag the background galaxy** (the yellow dot) yourself to directly behind the black hole, within 0.06 Einstein radii, so that its image closes into an **Einstein ring**.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.thuThach.goiY: The dashed blue line joins the observer to the black hole and continues behind it: bring the yellow dot to where that line crosses the source plane. The small panel under Controls shows the same scene.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.ten: The photon sphere: light going in circles
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
Zoom in close to the black hole. Lower the impact parameter to near **2.6 rs** and the deflection shoots up. At $b = 2{,}62\,r_s$ the ray swings through 252°, almost turning back. At $b = 2{,}6005\,r_s$ it winds **more than once around** before escaping. Below $2{,}598\,r_s$ the ray is swallowed.

The ray winds around at a radius of **1.5 rs**: the {{mặt cầu photon|photon sphere}} (the faint golden mesh). There light can travel in a circle. But that circle is **unstable**, like a marble balanced on a hilltop: the slightest offset and the ray either falls in or flies off.

$$ r_{\text{photon}} = \frac32\,r_s, \qquad b_c = \frac{3\sqrt3}{2}\,r_s \approx 2{,}598\,r_s $$

$b_c$ is the critical impact parameter. Notice that $b_c$ is larger than 1.5 rs: a ray arriving from far away is bent inward on the way, so its closest point lies deeper than its original impact parameter.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the blue dot very slowly toward the black hole and listen to the tone: near the threshold, the smallest nudge sends the deflection soaring. Use the arrow keys to nudge it bit by bit.
> [[b = 2.62 rs|s262]] [[b = 2.6005 rs: one full loop|s26]] [[b = 2.58 rs: swallowed|s258]]

+++ Going deeper: finding 1.5 rs and $3\sqrt3/2$
For light, proceed as in Lesson 13 but without the rest-mass term. Let $\lambda$ be a parameter along the ray:

$$ \Big(\frac{\dd r}{\dd\lambda}\Big)^2 + L^2\,\frac{1-r_s/r}{r^2} = E^2 $$

The function $W(r) = (1-r_s/r)/r^2$ plays the role of an effective potential. Setting its derivative to zero: $-2/r^3 + 3r_s/r^4 = 0$, so $r = \frac32 r_s$. The peak value: $W = \frac{1/3}{9/4}\,r_s^{-2} = \frac{4}{27}\,r_s^{-2}$.

A ray arriving from far away has $b = L/E$. It gets over the peak (and falls in) when $1/b^2 > 4/(27r_s^2)$, that is, $b \lt \sqrt{27/4}\,r_s = \frac{3\sqrt3}{2}\,r_s$.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.de: Drag the selected ray so that it **turns through exactly a right angle**: a 90° deflection (within 4°). How far is the impact parameter then from the threshold $b_c \approx 2{,}6\,r_s$?
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.goiY: Starting from $b = 2{,}62\,r_s$ (a 252° deflection), drag outward gradually. The right angle comes at about $b \approx 3{,}08\,r_s$, only some 0.5 $r_s$ above the threshold, whereas the weak-field formula $2r_s/b$ would need $b \approx 1{,}3\,r_s$.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.ten: Swallowed: the critical circle and the shadow
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
Look along the beam from the side of the light source. The red circle where the beam starts has a radius of exactly $b_c \approx 2{,}6\,r_s$. **Every ray that enters inside this circle falls into the black hole**, including rays that would have passed outside the horizon if space were flat. The red rays are those rays.

The area of the circle is $\pi b_c^2 = 6{,}75\,\pi r_s^2$: the black hole “catches” light like a disk nearly **seven times** the cross-section of its horizon.

Now reverse the direction: stand on the right and look toward the black hole. In directions inside the critical circle, tracing the light back we only reach the horizon, never a star. That is the black hole’s **shadow**, with a diameter of $2b_c = 3\sqrt3\,r_s \approx 5{,}2\,r_s$. Lesson 15 builds exactly that shadow.

> [Thử ngay] The sky behind shows that shadow too: a black disk almost three times as wide as the horizon sphere, rimmed by images of stars bent around the photon sphere.
> [[View from the light source|truoc]] [[View from behind|sau]] [[Oblique view|cheo]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.thuThach.de: Drag the selected ray inside the red circle so that it is **swallowed even though its impact parameter is still larger than $2{,}2\,r_s$**, well above the horizon radius ($r_s$) and the photon-sphere radius ($1{,}5\,r_s$).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.thuThach.goiY: The red circle has radius $b_c \approx 2{,}6\,r_s$. Put the blue dot inside the circle, near its edge: any impact parameter from 2.2 to 2.59 $r_s$ will do.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.noiDung:
Every phenomenon in this lesson comes from one fact: light follows geodesics with $\dd s^2 = 0$ in Schwarzschild spacetime.

| Phenomenon | Number | Measured by |
|---|---|---|
| Deflection at the Sun’s edge | 1.75″ (Newton 0.88″) | 1919 eclipse |
| Shapiro delay | about 250 µs (radar to Mars) | late 1960s; Cassini 2002 |
| Einstein ring | about 1″ to a few arcseconds for galaxies | Hubble, James Webb images |
| Photon sphere | 1.5 rs; critical impact parameter 2.6 rs | black-hole shadows, EHT 2019 and 2022 (Lesson 15) |

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] “Light has energy, energy is equivalent to mass, so light is pulled like a stone.” That argument gives only **half** the deflection, exactly Newton’s number. The other half appears in no “pulling force” picture at all: it is the curvature of space.

> [Thử ngay] [[See the whole beam again|cheo]] [[Larger mass|m2]]
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: $b$: impact parameter. At the Sun’s edge: 1.75″. Newton gives only half.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.4.y: The angular radius of the ring when source, lens and observer are lined up.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.5.ten: Photon sphere and critical impact parameter
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: A light ray passes the Sun at twice the Sun’s radius. What is its deflection?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: $\alpha = 2r_s/b$ is inversely proportional to $b$: double $b$ and the deflection halves, $1{,}75″/2 \approx 0{,}88″$. That it matches Newton’s number for a grazing ray is just a coincidence.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: Why is Einstein’s deflection twice the Newtonian value?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.1: Because light travels twice as fast as Newton’s bullet
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.2: Because curved time and curved space both bend the ray, each contributing half
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.3: Because the Sun is twice as heavy as Newton thought
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.4: Because light is bent twice: once on the way in and once on the way out
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: The curved-time part gives exactly Newton’s number (and the number Einstein obtained in 1911 from the equivalence principle alone). The curved-space part adds an equal amount. Bending “on the way in and on the way out” is already included in both calculations.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: During an eclipse, where does a star seen right at the Sun’s edge appear compared with its usual position?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.4: Split into two clearly separate stars
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: The light is bent toward the Sun. The eye looks back along the direction in which the light arrives, so it sees the star farther from the Sun. A second image (on the other side) does exist, but it lies deep inside the Sun’s disk and is extremely faint.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: A radar signal passing close to the Sun arrives a few hundred microseconds late. Which explanation is correct?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.1: Light slows down near the Sun; anyone measuring it there finds less than $c$
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.2: The Sun’s atmosphere slows radio waves; relativity has nothing to do with it
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.3: By the distant clock, a path through curved time and curved space takes longer; locally light still travels at exactly $c$
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.4: The signal has to take a detour tens of kilometers longer
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: Anyone standing still anywhere who measures the speed of light where they are gets $c$. The delay is an effect of geometry: clocks near the Sun run slow and rulers there are stretched relative to the coordinates of a distant observer. The longer path caused by bending contributes almost nothing. The Sun’s atmosphere does have a real effect, but it is separated out by using two frequencies.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: One gravitational lens is 4 times as massive as another, at the same distances. How many times larger is its Einstein ring?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.giai: $\theta_E \propto \sqrt{M}$, so 4 times the mass gives a ring radius $\sqrt4 = 2$ times larger. That is why measuring the size of an Einstein ring is a way to weigh a galaxy, including its dark matter, which gives off no light.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.hoi: A light ray has an impact parameter of 2.5 rs. If space were flat, it would pass 2.5 rs from the center, outside the horizon. Why is it still swallowed?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.dap: The critical impact parameter is $b_c = (3\sqrt3/2)\,r_s \approx 2{,}6\,r_s$. On its way in, the ray is bent inward more and more strongly, so its closest point drops below 2.5 rs. In terms of the “effective potential” for light, a ray with $b \lt b_c$ has more energy than the peak of the potential at the photon sphere (1.5 rs): nothing pushes it back out, so it goes straight on to the horizon.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.1: J. B. Hartle, *Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein’s General Relativity* (2003), chapter 9: the paths of light around a spherical mass; chapter 10: the bending of light, the Shapiro delay, gravitational lensing.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.2: F. W. Dyson, A. S. Eddington and C. Davidson, report on the eclipse expeditions of 29 May 1919 (1920).
bai.baiGiang.docThem.3: E. F. Taylor, J. A. Wheeler and E. Bertschinger, *Exploring Black Holes* (2nd edition): the paths of light around a black hole, the photon sphere.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.4: K. S. Thorne, *Black Holes and Time Warps* (1994): the story of the tests and of black-hole images, written for general readers.

bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.2.nghia: The distance from the center of the mass to the original (straight) line of flight of a light ray or of an object arriving from far away.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.3.nghia: A signal passing close to a mass arrives later, by the distant clock. Near the Sun the delay is a few hundred microseconds.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.4.nghia: The ring-shaped image of a light source lined up directly behind a gravitational lens.
